    Chapter 6

    Hash Functions: Digital Fingerprints

    🤔 Change one letter in a 4 GB movie and its fingerprint changes completely. Find two files with the same fingerprint and you can fake a Windows Update. 😱

    • ⏱️ ~6 min
    • 📚 9 sections
    • 🎮 3 interactive
    • ⭐ 220 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    6.1What a hash function does#

    A hash function takes any input (a word, a password, a 4 GB movie) and produces a short, fixed-size output called a hash, digest or fingerprint.

    Analogies:

    • 👆 A fingerprint: a tiny pattern that identifies a whole person, but you can't rebuild the person from the fingerprint.
    • 🥩 A meat grinder: easy to put a steak in and get mince out; impossible to turn mince back into the steak.
    ✔ section read

    6.2The avalanche effect#

    Change the input even slightly, and the output changes completely:

    One capital letter or one exclamation mark changes about half of the output bits. There's no way to tell from the hashes that the inputs were similar.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✔ section read

    6.3The properties of a good cryptographic hash#

    Property Plain meaning Analogy
    Deterministic Same input → same output, every time, on every computer Your fingerprint doesn't change
    Fixed size Output length never changes (SHA-256 is always 256 bits) Every fingerprint fits on the same card
    Fast Quick to compute (good for files; bad for passwords, see Chapter 8)
    Avalanche effect Tiny input change → completely different output
    Preimage resistance (one-way) Given a hash, you can't find an input that produces it Can't rebuild a person from a fingerprint
    Second-preimage resistance Given an input, you can't find a different input with the same hash Can't find a stranger with your exact fingerprint
    Collision resistance You can't find any two inputs with the same hash Can't find any two people with matching fingerprints
    ✔ section read

    6.4Collisions and the birthday paradox#

    There are infinitely many possible inputs and only 2²⁵⁶ possible SHA-256 outputs, so collisions must exist (two different inputs with the same hash). The pigeonhole principle guarantees it. The requirement is that nobody can ever find one.

    How hard is finding a collision? The birthday paradox gives a surprising answer:

    In a room of just 23 people, there's a better than 50% chance that two share a birthday.

    That seems too low because you're not looking for someone with your birthday; you're looking for any matching pair, and the number of pairs grows fast (23 people make 253 pairs).

    For hashes, it means you'll likely find a collision after about 2^(n/2) tries, not 2ⁿ. So:

    Hash Output size Collision resistance
    MD5 128 bits 2⁶⁴ in theory (and broken far below that in practice)
    SHA-1 160 bits 2⁸⁰ in theory (broken in practice)
    SHA-256 256 bits 2¹²⁸ ✅
    SHA-512 512 bits 2²⁵⁶ ✅

    That's why secure hashes have outputs twice as long as the security level they aim for.

    ✔ section read

    6.5The hash family tree#

    Hash Year Output size Status Notes
    MD5 1992 128 bits ❌ Broken Collisions can be found in seconds on a laptop. OK only for non-security checksums.
    SHA-1 1995 160 bits ❌ Broken First public collision in 2017 ("SHAttered"); being phased out everywhere
    SHA-2 family: SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 2001 224–512 bits ✅ Secure The workhorse of the internet: TLS, certificates, Bitcoin
    SHA-3 (Keccak) 2015 224–512 bits ✅ Secure Totally different internal design, a backup in case SHA-2 is ever broken
    BLAKE2 2012 up to 512 bits ✅ Secure Faster than MD5 while being secure; used in WireGuard, Argon2
    BLAKE3 2020 any length ✅ Secure Extremely fast and parallel

    📜 True story: SHAttered (2017). Researchers from Google and the CWI institute in Amsterdam created two different PDF files with the same SHA-1 hash. It took about 9 quintillion (9 × 10¹⁸) SHA-1 computations, roughly 6,500 years of single-CPU time. By 2020, a stronger "chosen-prefix" collision cost only around $45,000 in rented computing. SHA-1 is dead for security.

    📜 True story: the Flame malware (2012). A cyber-espionage tool called Flame used an MD5 collision to forge a Microsoft code-signing certificate. Infected computers accepted Flame as a genuine Windows Update. Weak hashes aren't a theoretical problem.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Hash functions

    ❌ Avoid
    MD5

    1992, 128-bit

    • Very fast
    • Fine as a non-security checksum
    • Collisions in seconds on a laptop
    • Used to forge a Microsoft certificate (Flame)
    Best for: Detecting accidental corruption only
    ❌ Avoid
    SHA-1

    1995, 160-bit

    • Still everywhere in old systems
    • SHAttered collision (2017)
    • Chosen-prefix collision for ~$45k (2020)
    Best for: Nothing new
    ✅ Use it
    SHA-256 / SHA-512

    SHA-2 family, 2001

    • The internet’s workhorse
    • Hardware support (SHA-NI)
    • No practical attacks
    • Length-extension attack (use HMAC)
    • Too fast for passwords
    Best for: TLS, certificates, Bitcoin, Git’s future
    ✅ Use it
    SHA-3

    Keccak sponge, 2015

    • Totally different design: a backup for SHA-2
    • Immune to length extension
    • Slower in software than SHA-2/BLAKE
    • Less hardware support
    Best for: Diversity; KMAC; new standards
    ✅ Use it
    BLAKE2

    2012

    • Faster than MD5, yet secure
    • Built-in keyed mode
    • Not a NIST standard (matters for FIPS)
    Best for: WireGuard, Argon2, file integrity
    ✅ Use it
    BLAKE3

    2020

    • Extremely fast and parallel
    • Any output length; built-in tree mode
    • Young; not FIPS
    • Smaller security margin (fewer rounds)
    Best for: Hashing huge files fast
    ✔ section read

    6.6How a hash works inside (very briefly)#

    SHA-2 (and MD5, SHA-1): the Merkle–Damgård design. The message is padded and cut into blocks. Each block is mixed into a running internal "state," like adding ingredients one at a time to a blender that never stops. The final state is the hash.

    ⚠️ This design has a quirk called the length-extension attack. Because the output is the final state, someone who knows SHA256(secret + message) can compute SHA256(secret + message + padding + extra) without knowing the secret. That's why "hash the secret together with the message" is not a safe way to authenticate messages. Use HMAC instead (Chapter 7).

    SHA-3: the sponge design. The input is "absorbed" into a big internal state, then the output is "squeezed" out. Part of the state is never output, which blocks length-extension attacks.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Hash designs

    👍 Situational
    Merkle–Damgård

    MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2

    • Simple, well understood
    • Proven: collision-resistant if the compression is
    • Output = internal state → length extension
    Best for: SHA-256 (with HMAC for keyed use)
    ✅ Use it
    Sponge

    SHA-3, absorb then squeeze

    • Hidden capacity blocks length extension
    • Flexible output length (SHAKE)
    • Large state; slower in software
    Best for: SHA-3, KMAC, ML-KEM internals
    ✔ section read

    6.7What hashes are used for#

    Use How
    Verifying downloads Compare the file's hash with the published one
    Digital signatures You sign the hash of a document, not the whole document (Chapter 11)
    Password storage Only with special slow hashes (Chapter 8)
    Git Every commit, file and folder is identified by its hash. Change one byte of history and every later ID changes.
    Blockchains Each block contains the hash of the previous one, forming a chain that can't be quietly edited
    Deduplication Cloud storage can detect identical files by hash and store them once
    Message authentication Inside HMAC (Chapter 7)
    Key derivation Inside HKDF, PBKDF2 (Chapter 8)
    Certificate Transparency Public logs of certificates organized as hash trees (Chapter 13)

    Merkle trees: hashing lots of data efficiently

    A Merkle tree hashes items in pairs, then hashes the pairs, and so on, until one root hash represents everything.

    If anything in A, B, C or D changes, the root changes. And you can prove that "C is included" by sharing just H4 and H12 rather than all the data. Bitcoin, Git, Certificate Transparency and many file-sync systems use Merkle trees.

    6.8Hands-on with hashes#

    🧪 Try it yourself (command line):

    Terminal
    # macOS / Linux: hash a short string (printf avoids adding a newline)
printf 'hello' | shasum -a 256
# 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824  -

# Same thing with OpenSSL
printf 'hello' | openssl dgst -sha256
# SHA2-256(stdin)= 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824

# Hash a file
shasum -a 256 some-download.iso          # macOS
sha256sum some-download.iso              # Linux
    PowerShell
    # Windows PowerShell
Get-FileHash .\some-download.iso -Algorithm SHA256

    ⚠️ echo "hello" adds an invisible newline character, so its hash is different (5891b5b5...). That catches many people out.

    Python
    import hashlib

for text in ["hello", "Hello", "hello!"]:
    print(f"{text:8} -> {hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()}")

# Hash a large file without loading it all into memory
h = hashlib.sha256()
with open("some-download.iso", "rb") as f:
    for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
        h.update(chunk)
print(h.hexdigest())

# Other algorithms
print(hashlib.sha3_256(b"hello").hexdigest())
print(hashlib.blake2b(b"hello", digest_size=32).hexdigest())

    Verifying a download properly. Linux distributions like Ubuntu publish a SHA256SUMS file next to their downloads:

    Terminal
    sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing
# ubuntu-24.04-desktop-amd64.iso: OK

    ⚠️ Watch out: if an attacker hacks the download site, they can replace both the file and the checksum. A checksum on the same page only protects against accidental corruption. That's why projects also digitally sign the checksum file (Chapter 11), and you verify the signature with a key you got some other way.

    ✔ section read

    6.9Common hash misconceptions#

    • ❌ "Hashing is encryption." No. There's no key and no way to "decrypt" a hash.
    • ❌ "Hashed data is anonymous." Not if the input is guessable. There are only about 10 billion 10-digit phone numbers. An attacker can hash them all in minutes and reverse any "anonymized" phone-number hash. Same for dates of birth, ID numbers, emails from a known list.
    • ❌ "MD5 is fine for passwords." It's a terrible choice twice over: broken and far too fast (Chapter 8).
    ✔ section read
